paragraphs: In the quest for the perfect lawn, homeowners across the country are taking a shortcut—and it is the environment that is paying the price. About eight million square metres of plastic grass is sold each year but opposition has now spread to the highest gardening circles. The Chelsea Flower Show has banned fake grass from this year’s event, declaring it to be not part of its ethos. The Royal Horticultural Society (RHS), which runs the annual show in west London, says it has introduced the ban because of the damage plastic grass does to the environment and biodiversity.

Ed Horne, of the RHS, said: “We launched our sustainability strategy last year and fake grass is just not in line with our ethos and views on plastic. We recommend using real grass because of its environmental benefits, which include supporting wildlife, alleviating flooding and cooling the environment.”

The RHS’s decision comes as campaigners try to raise awareness of the problems fake grass causes. A Twitter account, which claims to “cut through the greenwash” of artificial grass, already has more than 20,000 followers. It is trying to encourage people to sign two petitions, one calling for a ban on the sale of plastic grass and another calling for an “ecological damage” tax on such lawns. They have gathered 7,276 and 11,282 signatures.

However, supporters of fake grass point out that there is also an environmental impact with natural lawns, which need mowing and therefore usually consume electricity or petrol. The industry also points out that real grass requires considerable amounts of water, weed killer or other treatments and that people who lay fake grass tend to use their garden more. The industry also claims that people who lay fake grass spend an average of £500 on trees or shrubs for their garden, which provides habitat for insects.
In response to another petition last year about banning fake lawns, which gathered 30,000 signatures, the government responded that it has “no plans to ban the use of artificial grass”.

It added: “We prefer to help people and organisations make the right choice rather than legislating on such matters. However, the use of artificial grass must comply with the legal and policy safeguards in place to protect biodiversity and ensure sustainable drainage, while measures such as the strengthened biodiversity duty should serve to encourage public authorities to consider sustainable alternatives.”

It’s easy to dismiss as absurd the federal government’s ideas for plugging the chronic funding gap of our national parks. Can anyone really think it’s a good idea to allow Amazon deliveries to your tent in Yosemite or food trucks to line up under the redwood trees at Sequoia National Park?

But the government is right about one thing: U.S. national parks are in crisis. Collectively, they have a maintenance backlog of more than $12 billion. Roads, trails, restrooms, visitor centers and other infrastructure are crumbling.

But privatizing and commercializing the campgrounds would not be a cure-all. Campgrounds are a tiny portion of the overall infrastructure backlog, and businesses in the parks hand over, on average, only about 5% of their revenues to the National Park Service.

Moreover, increased privatization would certainly undercut one of the major reasons why 300 million visitors come to the parks each year: to enjoy nature and get a break from the commercial drumbeat that overwhelms daily life.

The real problem is that the parks have been chronically starved of funding. An economic survey of 700 U.S. taxpayers found that people would be willing to pay a significant amount of money to make sure the parks and their programs are kept intact. Some 81% of respondents said they would be willing to pay additional taxes for the next 10 years to avoid any cuts to the national parks.

The national parks provide great value to U.S. residents both as places to escape and as symbols of nature. On top of this, they produce value from their extensive educational programs, their positive impact on the climate through carbon sequestration, their contribution to our cultural and artistic life, and of course through tourism. The parks also help keep America’s past alive, working with thousands of local jurisdictions around the country to protect historical sites and to bring the stories of these places to life.

The parks do all this on a shoestring. Congress allocates only $3 billion a year to the national park system—an amount that has been flat since 2001 (in inflation-adjusted dollars) with the exception of a onetime boost in 2009. Meanwhile, the number of annual visitors has increased by more than 50% since 1980, and now stands at 330 million visitors per year.

The Internet may be changing merely what we remember, not our capacity to do so, suggests Columbia University psychology professor Betsy Sparrow. In 2011, Sparrow led a study in which participants were asked to record 40 factoids in a computer (“an ostrich’s eye is bigger than its brain,” for example). Half of the participants were told the information would be erased, while the other half were told it would be saved. Guess what? The latter group made no effort to recall the information when quizzed on it later, because they knew they could find it on their computers. In the same study, a group was asked to remember both the information and the folders it was stored in. They didn’t remember the information, but they remembered how to find the folders. In other words, human memory is not deteriorating but “adapting to new communications technology,” Sparrow says.

In a very practical way, the Internet is becoming an external hard drive for our memories, a process known as “cognitive offloading.” Traditionally, this role was fulfilled by data banks, libraries, and other humans. Your father may never remember birthdays because your mother does, for instance. Some worry that this is having a destructive effect on society, but Sparrow sees an upside. Perhaps, she suggests, the trend will change our approach to learning from a focus on individual facts and memorization to an emphasis on more conceptual thinking—something that is not available on the Internet. “I personally have never seen all that much intellectual value in memorizing things,” Sparrow says, adding that we haven’t lost our ability to do it.

Still other experts say it’s too soon to understand how the Internet affects our brains. There is no experimental evidence showing that it interferes with our ability to focus, for instance, wrote psychologists Christopher Chabris and Daniel J. Simons. And surfing the web exercised the brain more than reading did among computer-savvy older adults in a 2008 study involving 24 participants at the Semel Institute for Neuroscience and Human Behavior at the University of California, Los Angeles.

“There may be costs associated with our increased reliance on the Internet, but I’d have to imagine that overall the benefits are going to outweigh those costs,” observes psychology professor Benjamin Storm. “It seems pretty clear that memory is changing, but is it changing for the better? At this point, we don’t know.”

Teenagers are paradoxical. That’s a mild and detached way of saying something that parents often express with considerably stronger language. But the paradox is scientific as well as personal. In adolescence, helpless and dependent children who have relied on grown-ups for just about everything become independent people who can take care of themselves and help each other. At the same time, once cheerful and compliant children become rebellious teenage risk-takers.

A new study published in the journal Child Development, by Eveline Crone of the University of Leiden and colleagues, suggests that the positive and negative sides of teenagers go hand in hand. The study is part of a new wave of thinking about adolescence. For a long time, scientists and policy makers concentrated on the idea that teenagers were a problem that needed to be solved. The new work emphasizes that adolescence is a time of opportunity as well as risk.

The researchers studied “prosocial” and rebellious traits in more than 200 children and young adults, ranging from 11 to 28 years old. The participants filled out questionnaires about how often they did things that were altruistic and positive, like sacrificing their own interests to help a friend, or rebellious and negative, like getting drunk or staying out late.

Other studies have shown that rebellious behavior increases as you become a teenager and then fades away as you grow older. But the new study shows that, interestingly, the same pattern holds for prosocial behavior. Teenagers were more likely than younger children or adults to report that they did things like unselfishly help a friend.

Most significantly, there was a positive correlation between prosociality and rebelliousness. The teenagers who were more rebellious were also more likely to help others. The good and bad sides of adolescence seem to develop together.

Is there some common factor that underlies these apparently contradictory developments? One idea is that teenage behavior is related to what researchers call “reward sensitivity.” Decision-making always involves balancing rewards and risks, benefits and costs. “Reward sensitivity” measures how much reward it takes to outweigh risk.

Teenagers are particularly sensitive to social rewards—winning the game, impressing a new friend, getting that boy to notice you. Reward sensitivity, like prosocial behavior and risk-taking, seems to go up in adolescence and then down again as we age. Somehow, when you hit 30, the chance that something exciting and new will happen at that party just doesn’t seem to outweigh the effort of getting up off the couch.

context.text: … The Royal Horticultural Society (RHS), which runs the annual show in west London, ==says it has introduced the ban **because of the damage plastic grass does to the environment** and biodiversity.==
Ed Horne, of the RHS, said: “We launched our sustainability strategy last year and ==fake grass is just **not in line with** our ethos and views on plastic==. …

questions.stem: The RHS thinks that plastic grass ______.

options.B: is a hot topic in gardening circles
options.C: is overpraised in the annual show
options.D: is ruining the view of west London

basis: 题干问 RHS（皇家园艺学会）的看法，定位第一段末句：学会说之所以颁布禁令，是因为塑料草对环境和生物多样性造成的破坏（the damage … does to the environment）。第二段学会的 Ed Horne 又补充：假草不符合学会的理念和对塑料的看法。
map: the damage plastic grass does to the environment

wrong.text: 第一段说反对之声已蔓延到园艺界最高层（the highest gardening circles），讲的是反对扩散，不是 RHS 认为塑料草是“热门话题”。
花展是禁止假草参展，没说它在展会上被过度赞扬。
west London 只是花展举办地点，与景观无关。

context.text: … It is trying to encourage people to sign two petitions, ==one calling for **a ban on the sale of plastic grass** and another calling for an **“ecological damage” tax** on such lawns==. They have gathered 7,276 and 11,282 signatures.

questions.stem: The petitions mentioned in Paragraph 3 reveal the campaigners’ ______.

options.B: resistance to fake grass use
options.C: anger over the proposed tax

basis: 第三段两份请愿：一份要求禁售塑料草，一份要求对假草坪征收“生态损害”税。一个要禁，一个要征税，都是在阻止人们用假草，所以体现的是活动人士对假草的抵制。
map: a ban on the sale of plastic grass / “ecological damage” tax

wrong.text: RHS 禁了假草，和活动人士立场一致，谈不上失望。
征税正是活动人士自己提出的，他们支持而不是愤怒。
他们担心的是假草的危害，不是真草的供应。

context.text: However, supporters of fake grass point out that ==there is also an environmental impact with natural lawns, which **need mowing** and therefore usually **consume electricity or petrol**==. The industry also points out that ==real grass **requires considerable amounts of water**, weed killer or other treatments== and that people who lay fake grass tend to use their garden more. …

questions.stem: In Paragraph 4, supporters of fake grass point out ______.

options.A: the necessity to lower the costs of fake grass
options.B: the disadvantages of growing real grass
options.C: the way to take care of artificial lawns
options.D: the challenges of insect habitat protection

basis: 第四段用 However 转到假草支持者：天然草坪也影响环境，要修剪、耗电耗油；真草还需要大量的水、除草剂等。这些都是在列举种真草的弊端。
map: need mowing … consume electricity or petrol / requires considerable amounts of water
the disadvantages of growing real grass

wrong.text: 没有提到降低假草的成本。
原文讲的是真草需要修剪、浇水、除草，不是如何打理人造草坪。
昆虫栖息地出现在段末，是支持者说铺假草的人会买树木灌木、给昆虫提供栖息地，是好处，不是保护栖息地的挑战。

context.text: … the government responded that it has ==“**no plans to ban** the use of artificial grass”==.

It added: “==We prefer to help people and organisations make the right choice **rather than legislating** on such matters.== However, ==the use of artificial grass **must comply with** the legal and policy safeguards **in place**== to protect biodiversity and ensure sustainable drainage …

questions.stem: What would the government do with regard to artificial grass?

options.A: Urge legislation to restrict its use.
options.B: Take measures to guarantee its quality.
options.C: Remind its users to obey existing rules.

questions.answerZh: 提醒使用者遵守现有规定
basis: 第五段政府明确表态不打算禁用假草；第六段说更愿意帮人们做出正确选择，而不是立法；接着 However 一转：使用人造草必须遵守现行的（in place）法律和政策保障。这就是提醒使用者遵守已有规定。
map: the legal and policy safeguards in place

wrong.text: 政府说的是 rather than legislating，不打算立法限制。
没提保证假草质量。
原文是鼓励公共机构“考虑”可持续替代方案（consider sustainable alternatives），不是政府要用替代品取代假草。

context.text: … About eight million square metres of plastic grass is sold each year but ==**opposition** has now spread to the highest gardening circles==. The Chelsea Flower Show has banned fake grass from this year’s event, declaring it to be not part of its ethos. The Royal Horticultural Society (RHS), which runs the annual show in west London, says it has introduced the ban because of the damage plastic grass does to the environment and biodiversity.
==However, **supporters of fake grass** point out== that there is also an environmental impact with natural lawns, which need mowing and therefore usually consume electricity or petrol. …

questions.stem: It can be learned from the text that fake grass ______.

options.B: has seen a market share decline
options.C: is becoming increasingly affordable

basis: 全文主旨题。一方是反对者：RHS 禁止参展、活动人士发起请愿、要求禁售和征税；另一方是支持者：行业指出真草也有环境代价；政府则不禁止、只要求守规。有人反对、有人支持，假草就是一个有争议的产品。

wrong.text: 全文没有讲假草在技术上不断改进。
只说每年卖出约八百万平方米，没有市场份额下降的数据。
没有讲价格；£500 是铺假草的人买树木灌木的花费，与假草价格无关。

context.text: But the government is right about one thing: U.S. national parks are in crisis. ==Collectively, they have a **maintenance backlog** of more than $12 billion.== ==Roads, trails, restrooms, visitor centers and other **infrastructure are crumbling**.==

questions.stem: What problem are U.S. national parks faced with?

options.B: Inadequate commercialization.
options.C: Lack of transportation services.

basis: 第二段直接说国家公园处于危机中：维护工作积压的资金缺口超过 120 亿美元，道路、步道、卫生间、游客中心等基础设施正在破败。维护积压、设施破败，就是基础设施维护不善。

wrong.text: 第三段说公园里的企业只把约 5% 的收入交给管理局，讲的是上交比例低，不是企业利润下降。
作者恰恰反对靠商业化解决问题，认为它不是万能药，还会破坏游客体验。
亚马逊送快递到帐篷是政府被嘲讽的点子，不是说公园缺交通服务。

context.text: … ==increased privatization would certainly **undercut** one of the major reasons why 300 million visitors come to the parks each year: **to enjoy nature and get a break from the commercial drumbeat** that overwhelms daily life.==

questions.stem: Increased privatization of the campgrounds may ______.

options.B: help preserve nature
options.C: bring operational pressure

basis: 第四段：加大私有化必然会削弱（undercut）游客来公园的主要原因之一，即享受自然、暂时摆脱日常生活里铺天盖地的商业气息。来公园的目的被破坏，就是游客体验被破坏。
map: to enjoy nature and get a break from the commercial drumbeat

wrong.text: 私有化会让人难以享受自然，不是有助于保护自然。
没有提运营压力。
削弱了游客来访的理由，不会促进访问量。

context.text: … An economic survey of 700 U.S. taxpayers found that people would be willing to pay a significant amount of money to make sure the parks and their programs are kept intact. ==**Some 81% of respondents** said they would be **willing to pay additional taxes** for the next 10 years to avoid any cuts to the national parks.==

questions.stem: According to Paragraph 5, most respondents in the survey would ______.

options.A: go to the national parks on a regular basis
options.B: advocate a bigger budget for the national parks
options.C: agree to pay extra for the national parks
options.D: support the national parks’ recent reforms

questions.answerZh: 同意为国家公园额外付费
basis: 第五段调查：约 81% 的受访者（most respondents）表示愿意在今后 10 年多缴税，以免国家公园经费被削减。愿意多缴税就是同意为国家公园额外付费。

wrong.text: 调查问的是愿不愿意出钱，不是会不会经常去。
受访者说的是自己愿意多付钱，不是倡导国会扩大预算。增加预算是作者在最后一段暗示的结论，不是受访者的表态。
文中没提公园最近有什么改革。

context.text: … ==The parks also help **keep America’s past alive**, working with thousands of local jurisdictions around the country to **protect historical sites**== and to bring the stories of these places to life.

questions.stem: The national parks are valuable in that they ______.

options.B: have historical significance
options.C: sponsor research on climate
options.D: provide an income for the locals

basis: 第六段逐项列公园的价值，最后一句：公园还帮助让美国的过去“活着”，与各地合作保护历史遗迹、讲述这些地方的故事。这就是具有历史意义。
map: keep America’s past alive / protect historical sites

wrong.text: 旅游只是公园产生价值的途径之一（of course through tourism），没说公园在旅游业中领先。
原文是公园通过固碳对气候有积极影响，不是资助气候研究。
与地方管辖机构合作是为了保护历史遗迹，没说给当地人提供收入。

context.text: ==The real problem is that the parks have been **chronically starved of funding**.== …

==The parks do all this **on a shoestring**.== Congress allocates only $3 billion a year to the national park system—==an amount that has been **flat** since 2001== (in inflation-adjusted dollars) with the exception of a onetime boost in 2009. Meanwhile, ==the number of annual visitors has **increased by more than 50%** since 1980==, and now stands at 330 million visitors per year.

questions.stem: It can be concluded from the text that the national park system ______.

options.A: is able to cope with staff shortages
options.B: is able to meet visitors’ demands
options.C: is in need of a new pricing policy
options.D: is in need of a funding increase

basis: 第五段点明真正的问题是公园长期缺钱（chronically starved of funding）。最后一段又说公园靠极少的钱（on a shoestring）做这么多事：国会拨款自 2001 年起基本没涨，游客却比 1980 年多了 50% 以上。钱不涨、人在涨，结论就是需要增加资金。
map: chronically starved of funding / on a shoestring
in need of a funding increase

wrong.text: 全文没有提员工短缺。
基础设施在破败、游客在增加、经费却不涨，说明难以满足游客需求。
没有讨论门票或定价；调查讲的是多缴税。

context.text: ==The Internet may be **changing merely what we remember**, **not our capacity** to do so==, suggests Columbia University psychology professor Betsy Sparrow. In 2011, Sparrow led a study in which participants were asked to record 40 factoids in a computer (“an ostrich’s eye is bigger than its brain,” for example). Half of the participants were told the information would be erased, while the other half were told it would be saved. Guess what? The latter group made no effort to recall the information when quizzed on it later, because they knew they could find it on their computers. In the same study, a group was asked to remember both the information and the folders it was stored in. ==They didn’t remember the information, but they **remembered how to find the folders**.== …

questions.stem: Sparrow’s study shows that with the Internet, the human brain will ______.

options.B: collect information efficiently
options.C: switch its focus of memory

basis: 首句就是 Sparrow 的结论：互联网改变的只是我们记什么，而不是记忆的能力。实验里，知道信息会被保存的人不去记信息本身；要求同时记信息和文件夹的人，没记住信息，却记住了怎么找文件夹。记的东西从“内容”变成了“去哪儿找”，就是记忆的重点转移了。

wrong.text: 实验没有涉及详细分析信息。
参与者记住的是信息存在哪里，不是更高效地收集信息。
原文说记忆能力没变（not our capacity），没说记忆时间会延长。

context.text: In a very practical way, ==the Internet is becoming **an external hard drive for our memories**, a process known as “cognitive offloading.”== Traditionally, this role was fulfilled by data banks, libraries, and other humans. ==Your father may never remember birthdays **because your mother does**, for instance.== …

questions.stem: The process of “cognitive offloading” ______.

options.B: keeps our memory from failing
options.C: enables us to classify trivial facts

basis: “认知卸载”就是把互联网当作记忆的外接硬盘。传统上这个角色由数据库、图书馆和别人承担，比如爸爸从来不记生日，因为妈妈记着。把要记的东西交给外部去存，就是减轻自己的记忆负担。offload 本义就是“卸下负担”。
map: an external hard drive for our memories

wrong.text: 没有提识别虚假信息。
“记忆没有退化”是 Sparrow 对实验结果的解读，认知卸载讲的是把记忆交给外部，不是防止记忆衰退。
实验里的 factoids 是琐碎事实，但没说认知卸载帮我们给它们分类。

context.text: … ==Some worry that this is having a destructive effect on society, **but Sparrow sees an upside**.== Perhaps, she suggests, ==the trend will **change our approach to learning** from a focus on individual facts and memorization to an emphasis on more conceptual thinking==—something that is not available on the Internet. “I personally have never seen all that much intellectual value in memorizing things,” Sparrow says, adding that we haven’t lost our ability to do it.

questions.stem: Which of the following would Sparrow support about the Internet?

options.A: It may reform our learning approach.
options.B: It may impact our society negatively.
options.C: It may enhance our adaptability to technology.
options.D: It may interfere with our conceptual thinking.

questions.answerZh: 它可能改革我们的学习方式
basis: 有人担心认知卸载对社会有破坏作用，但 Sparrow 看到了好的一面：这一趋势或许会把学习方式从注重单个事实和死记，转向更注重概念性思维。change our approach to learning 就是改革学习方式。

wrong.text: 认为对社会有破坏作用的是 Some（一些人），Sparrow 恰恰持相反态度。
第一段说的是人类记忆在“适应新的通讯技术”，是记忆在适应，不是互联网提高了我们对技术的适应能力。
Sparrow 认为学习会更强调概念性思维，而且这种思维是互联网上没有的，不是互联网干扰它。

context.text: ==Still other experts say it’s **too soon to understand** how the Internet affects our brains.== ==There is **no experimental evidence**== showing that it interferes with our ability to focus, for instance, wrote psychologists Christopher Chabris and Daniel J. Simons. …

questions.stem: It is indicated in Paragraph 3 that how the Internet affects our brains ______.

options.B: is most studied in older adults
options.C: is reflected in our reading speed

questions.answerZh: 需要进一步的学术研究
basis: 第三段首句是段落主旨：还有专家说，要弄清互联网如何影响大脑还为时过早。接着举例：没有实验证据表明上网会干扰专注力。现在下结论太早、证据不足，就是需要进一步研究。
map: too soon to understand / no experimental evidence

wrong.text: 只提到 2008 年一项 24 人参与的老年人研究，不能说老年人被研究得最多。
那项研究比较的是上网和阅读哪个更能锻炼大脑，与阅读速度无关。
没有说影响取决于上网习惯。

context.text: … In other words, ==human memory is **not deteriorating**== but “adapting to new communications technology,” Sparrow says.

“There may be costs associated with our increased reliance on the Internet, ==but I’d have to imagine that overall **the benefits are going to outweigh those costs**==,” observes psychology professor Benjamin Storm. …

questions.stem: Neither Sparrow nor Storm would agree that ______.

options.A: our reliance on the Internet will be costly
options.B: the Internet is weakening our memory
options.C: memory exercise is a must for our brains
options.D: our ability to focus declines with age

questions.answerZh: 互联网正在削弱我们的记忆力
basis: Sparrow 明确说人类记忆没有退化（not deteriorating），只是在适应新技术；Storm 认为总体来看依赖互联网的好处会超过代价。两人对互联网与记忆都持积极态度，都不会同意“互联网在削弱记忆力”。
map: （不同意）the Internet is weakening our memory
questions.note: Neither … nor … would agree 是反向题：找两人都反对的说法。先确认两人的共同立场（都看好互联网对记忆的影响），再找与之相反的选项。

wrong.text: Storm 承认 There may be costs，他会部分同意依赖互联网有代价，所以不是两人都不同意。
Sparrow 认为死记硬背没多大价值，但没讨论“记忆锻炼”；Storm 也没谈，无法判断两人都反对。
专注力是第三段 Chabris 和 Simons 谈的，而且没有涉及年龄。

context.text: ==Teenagers are **paradoxical**.== That’s a mild and detached way of saying something that parents often express with considerably stronger language. But the paradox is scientific as well as personal. In adolescence, ==**helpless and dependent** children who have relied on grown-ups for just about everything become **independent** people== who can take care of themselves and help each other. At the same time, ==once **cheerful and compliant** children become **rebellious** teenage risk-takers==.

questions.stem: According to Paragraph 1, children growing into adolescence tend to ______.

options.B: see the world in an unreasonable way
options.C: have fond memories of their past

questions.answerZh: 发展出相反的性格特征
basis: 首句定调：青少年是矛盾的（paradoxical）。后面给出两组变化：无助依赖的孩子变得独立、能照顾自己和帮助别人；与此同时，原本开朗顺从的孩子变成叛逆、爱冒险的青少年。一边变好、一边变“坏”，同时发展出相反的性格特征。

wrong.text: 没说青少年看待世界的方式不合理。
没有提对过去的回忆。
第二句说父母常用强烈得多的言辞形容青少年，是父母的抱怨，不是孩子对父母表达爱意。

context.text: … ==The study is part of **a new wave of thinking** about adolescence.== For a long time, scientists and policy makers concentrated on the idea that teenagers were a problem that needed to be solved. ==The new work emphasizes that adolescence is a time of **opportunity as well as risk**.==

questions.stem: It can be learned from Paragraph 2 that Crone’s study ______.

options.B: examines teenagers’ emotional problems
options.C: provides a new insight into adolescence

questions.answerZh: 为认识青春期提供了新视角
basis: 第二段说 Crone 的研究属于关于青春期的“新一波思考”。过去科学家和政策制定者把青少年看作需要解决的问题；新研究强调青春期既有风险也是机遇。这就是对青春期的新见解。
map: a new wave of thinking about adolescence

wrong.text: 没有讨论青少年的社会责任。
研究的是亲社会和叛逆行为，不是情绪问题。
只看负面、把青少年当问题是旧观点；新研究强调正负两面并存，还有机遇。

context.text: Other studies have shown that ==rebellious behavior **increases as you become a teenager** and then **fades away as you grow older**==. But the new study shows that, interestingly, ==**the same pattern** holds for prosocial behavior==. ==Teenagers were **more likely than younger children or adults** to report== that they did things like unselfishly help a friend. …

questions.stem: What does Crone’s study find about prosocial behavior?

options.A: It results from the wish to cooperate.
options.B: It is cultivated through education.
options.C: It is subject to family influence.
options.D: It tends to peak in adolescence.

questions.answerZh: 往往在青春期达到顶峰
basis: 第四段：其他研究发现，叛逆行为进入青春期时增多，长大后消退。新研究发现亲社会行为也是同样的模式（the same pattern），青少年比更小的孩子和成年人更常做无私帮助朋友这类事。先升后降、青春期最多，就是在青春期达到顶峰。最后一段也印证：奖励敏感度和亲社会行为、冒险一样，青春期上升、之后下降。
map: the same pattern（青春期增多，之后消退）

wrong.text: 没有说亲社会行为源于合作的愿望。
没有提教育。
没有提家庭影响。

context.text: ==Teenagers are **particularly sensitive to social rewards**—winning the game, impressing a new friend, getting that boy to notice you.== Reward sensitivity, like prosocial behavior and risk-taking, seems to go up in adolescence and then down again as we age. …

questions.stem: It can be learned from the last two paragraphs that teenagers ______.

options.B: care a lot about social recognition
options.C: become anxious about their future
options.D: endeavor to live a joyful life

basis: 倒数第二段引出“奖励敏感度”；最后一段说青少年对社交奖励特别敏感，例子是赢得比赛、给新朋友留下好印象、让那个男孩注意到你，都是想得到别人的认可。所以青少年非常在意社会认可。
map: care a lot about social recognition

wrong.text: 给新朋友留下印象是青少年想得到的奖励，不是夸大自己对别人的影响。
没有提对未来的焦虑。
派对上会发生新鲜刺激事情的例子说的是 30 岁以后的人懒得起身，用来对比奖励敏感度下降，不是说青少年努力过快乐的生活。

context.text: ==Teenagers are **paradoxical**.== …

Most significantly, ==there was a **positive correlation** between prosociality and rebelliousness==. The teenagers who were more rebellious were also more likely to help others. The good and bad sides of adolescence seem to develop together. …
==Is there some **common factor** that underlies these apparently **contradictory developments**?== …

questions.stem: What is the text mainly about?

options.B: Why teenagers are risk-sensitive.
options.C: How teenagers develop prosociality.

questions.answerZh: 青少年为什么自相矛盾
basis: 首句提出论点：青少年是矛盾的。中间用 Crone 的研究说明正面和负面特质同时发展、而且正相关；第六段问这些看似矛盾的发展背后是否有共同因素，再用“奖励敏感度”来解释。全文就是在讲青少年为什么会自相矛盾。

wrong.text: 文章讲的是对奖励（reward）敏感，而且尤其是社交奖励，不是对风险敏感。
亲社会性只是矛盾的一面，文章同时讲叛逆。
变得独立只在第一段作为例子出现。
